subject: physics_2
question_text: Three capacitors each of capacitance 9 pF are connected in series. (a) What is the total capacitance of the combination? (b) What is the potential difference across each capacitor, if the combination is connected to a 120 V supply?

verification.note: The 2+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Two structural checks are IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the two-book union check (the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only) and the past-paper back-test (the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers). Hand-checked against the book: 1/C = 3/9 gives C = 3 pF; Q = 3 pF × 120 V = 360 pC; V across each = 360 pC / 9 pF = 40 V and 3 × 40 = 120 V — every printed figure is correct. Transcription: the printed misspelling 'capcitance' is corrected to 'capacitance'; the printed spaces before the question marks are dropped. The book also prints a bold solving hint after the question ('Use the formula of equivalent capacitance when two or more capacitors are connected in series and remember that charges at the plates of each capacitor in series remain same.') — that is guidance, not part of the asked question, so it is not in question_text. This item is answered under 'Sol.' rather than the book's usual 'A.'

steps.margin_note: Third mark. Use the equivalent C, not 9 pF, to get the charge.
steps.why: The inner plates of a series chain are isolated, so whatever charge leaves one plate arrives on the next, so a single charge value applies to the whole chain.
common_mistakes: Using 9 pF instead of the equivalent 3 pF and getting 1080 pC.
Working out three different charges — in series there is only one.

recall.must_convey: That the charge is common in series and equals CV = 3 pF × 120 V = 360 pC.

steps.memory_tip: Series: one charge for all, the voltage splits.

steps.margin_note: Last mark. Divide by 9 pF, not 3 pF, and add the three back to 120 V.
steps.why: Equal capacitors carrying the same charge must share the supply voltage equally, so the check 3 × 40 = 120 V is the fastest proof the arithmetic is sound.

recall.must_convey: That V = Q/C = 360 pC / 9 pF = 40 V across each capacitor, and the three add to 120 V.

steps.memory_tip: Equal capacitors in series split the supply equally: 120 V over three is 40 V.

insider_note: The last mark turns on which capacitance is used in V = Q/C — the equivalent 3 pF gives the charge, but the individual 9 pF gives the potential difference.
